title: Burden sharing beyond budgets: Japan’s Official Security Assistance
author: IISS
text:
Darshana M. Baruah @darshanabaruahAbout Darshana M.

Online Analysis30th July 2026

Burden sharing beyond budgets: Japan’s Official Security AssistanceAmid rising tensions in the Indo-Pacific, Japan’s Official Security Assistance policy could play an important role in regional burden sharing through targeted investments in its partners’ defence capabilities.

For decades, since it was announced in 1954, Japan’s Overseas Development Assistance (ODA) has been one of its most successful economic, social and foreign policy initiatives. The ODA’s signature is that it is strictly designed for non-military purposes. In 2023, changes in its security environment urged Japan to launch the Official Security Assistance (OSA) programme. Unlike the ODA, the OSA can provide assistance to foreign armed forces and their associated agencies. OSA’s budget for FY2025 stood at 8.1 billion yen (approximately US$49 million); however, the budget was increased to 18.1bn yen (approximately US$116m) for FY2026. This move signals the increased value of the OSA in recent Japanese strategic calculations. Led by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, the OSA bridges converging strategic interests between wider Japanese security and military concerns.
A strategic shift
A primary aim of the initiative is to ‘partner countries with a view to strengthening their security and deterrence capabilities’. While the specifics of OSA projects are decided following conversations with partner states about their requirements, Japan has a special focus on providing equipment and supplies that help support or complement deterrence capabilities. For example, some of the approved projects include providing grants for uninhabited aerial vehicles (UAVs) for monitoring and surveillance purposes, such as to Sri Lanka and Tonga in 2025, as well as for a coastal radar system for Djibouti in 2024. At a broader level, these initiatives do not depict the traditional strategic conversation on building ‘deterrence’, as conventional deterrence is associated with military or war-fighting capability. Japan, however, appears to be taking a broader framing of deterrence, as its OSA projects largely provide enabling capabilities such as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, maritime-domain awareness and communications, rather than offensive weapons. Those capabilities improve a state’s ability to understand its security environment and make informed decisions. As such, investing in domestic capabilities to analyse the regional security landscape allows for more effective contributions to regional defence and security.
At the 2026 IISS Shangri-La Dialogue, Japanese Minister of Defense Koizumi Shinjirō linked the OSA with regional security, noting, ‘the aim of these initiatives is to tangibly strengthen deterrence and response capabilities of the region’. Along with some examples on defence collaboration, he further noted, ‘These are the efforts to support each country to choose for itself, to defend itself and to contribute to regional stability’. Koizumi’s speech underlines two themes which have appeared consistently in Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s recent remarks on the region and the Indo-Pacific: resilience through stronger defence capabilities and autonomy through states’ ability to make sovereign security choices. At a time of increasing fragmentation and continuing calls from the United States for partners and allies to do more to contribute toward regional security, OSA’s focus on resilience and deterrence-building capabilities could become an important pillar, as the Indo-Pacific debates the next security architecture.
Modest means, big impact and small states
A potential critique of OSA is the scale and scope of its projects being considered too small to have a true impact on deterrence building. A US$116m annual budget has limitations and will not address some of the biggest threats facing the Indo-Pacific. However, it does have the potential to be strategically significant, depending on what equipment it provides to which countries. For example, Japan provided Fiji with an approximate 400m yen grant for patrol boats and underwater cameras, among other equipment, in 2023. The value was over six times Fiji’s expenditure for capital purchase in 2023. Similarly, the value of grants to Papua New Guinea in 2025 was equivalent to 50% of the Papua New Guinea Ministry of Defence’s plant, machinery and equipment budget that same year. The choice of equipment, from UAVs to patrol boats to coastal radar systems, all contribute toward building both capacity and maritime domain awareness, a priority of the OSA initiative. Furthermore, in 2026, the OSA announced its first trilateral project with Australia to redevelop a battalion headquarters in Fiji. Tokyo is likely to pursue similar initiatives with other Quad partners (the US and India) in utilising the OSA.
As such, the strategic application of the OSA, with a focus on small island states and collaboration with Indo-Pacific partners, can deliver significant projects addressing capacity gaps in the Indo-Pacific maritime domain, despite its modest budget.
Conclusion
Viewed alongside Japan’s gradual relaxation of defence export restrictions and its willingness to pursue defence-industrial cooperation, including the prospective export of Mogami-class frigates, OSA represents one component of a wider strategic shift. Together, these initiatives broaden the range of security tools that Japan can offer to regional partners.
As the US continues to ask allies and partners to shoulder greater responsibility for regional security, burden sharing will increasingly be measured not only by defence spending but also by states’ ability to contribute meaningfully to regional stability. The OSA could offer additional resources: strengthening states’ capacity to secure themselves, enhancing collective maritime awareness and creating the conditions for more effective cooperation among partners. Rather than the scale of its assistance, what may yet define Japan’s contribution is its ability to strengthen regional autonomy in ways that make collective deterrence more credible and more sustainable.  

AuthorDarshana M. Baruah Shangri-La Dialogue Senior Fellow for Indo-Pacific Defence and Strategy
